blocks.text: So far our programs run straight from top to bottom, doing every line in order. Conditionals let them make choices: do this when something is true, and otherwise do that.

blocks.alt: Conditionals: if, if-else, else-if ladder, switch

blocks.text: This is a huge step. A program that can make decisions can react differently to different situations, which is what makes software feel intelligent.
A conditional is just your program asking a yes or no question and then acting on the answer. Every decision in every app comes down to this.
A condition is any expression that ends up being true or false. It is the boolean we met in the operators lesson.

codes.python:
age = 20
print(age >= 18)     # True, this is a condition

blocks.text: Conditions are usually comparisons, like age is at least 18, but any true or false value works. The program looks at the condition and decides what to do based on the answer.
The if Statement
This is the simplest decision. The code inside runs only when the condition is true, and is skipped otherwise.
Notice the structure: the word if, a condition, and then a block of code that runs only when the condition holds. In Python the block is set off by indentation, in Java and C++ by curly braces.
Add an else to handle the case when the condition is false. Exactly one of the two branches always runs.
Think of it as a fork in the road. The condition decides which path the program takes, and there is always exactly one path chosen.
Checking Many Cases
When there are several possibilities, chain the conditions together. The program checks them from top to bottom and runs the first one that is true, then skips the rest.
Order matters. Put the highest or most specific conditions first, because the program stops at the first match it finds. If you reverse the order, everyone might get a Grade C.
Any comparison operator can drive a condition. Here are the everyday ones in action.
Remember to use two equals signs to compare. A single equals sign is assignment and will either error or misbehave inside a condition.
Combining Conditions
Use logical operators to test more than one thing at once. This often reads better than many separate ifs.

codes.python:
age = 20
country = "India"
day = "Saturday"

if age >= 18 and country == "India":
    print("Eligible to vote in India")

if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday":
    print("It is the weekend")

blocks.text: Use and when every part must be true, and or when any one part is enough. This lets you express real world rules directly.
You can place one condition inside another. This is useful when a second question only makes sense after the first is answered.
Try not to nest too deeply. If you find yourself three or four levels in, see whether combining conditions with and, or returning early, can flatten it out.
Handling Edge Cases First
A clean style is to check the simple or invalid cases first and handle them right away. This keeps the main logic from drowning in nested ifs.
By dealing with the special cases up front and stopping early, the important code stays at the left margin where it is easy to read.
When you only need to choose between two values, many languages offer a one line shortcut for a simple if and else.

codes.python:
age = 20
status = "Adult" if age >= 18 else "Minor"
print(status)

blocks.text: Use it for short, simple choices where it stays readable. For anything complex, a full if and else is clearer and kinder to the reader.
Choosing Among Many Fixed Values
When you compare one value against many fixed options, some languages offer a switch or match statement. It can read more cleanly than a long chain of elifs.

codes.python:
command = "start"

# Python match, one of several equal options
match command:
    case "start":
        print("Starting")
    case "stop":
        print("Stopping")
    case _:
        print("Unknown command")

blocks.text: You can always use if and elif instead. Switch and match are just a tidier way to say the same thing when checking one value against a list of possibilities.
Many languages let you use non boolean values in a condition. They treat some values as true and others as false.

items: Empty things are usually false: an empty string, an empty list, the number zero.
Non empty things are usually true: any non zero number, any text with characters.

blocks.text: This is handy for quick checks like "if the list is not empty", but it can surprise beginners. When unsure, compare explicitly, such as if len(name) > 0.
Common Decision Patterns
A few small decision problems show up again and again. Recognising them makes you faster.

items: Even or odd: check number % 2 equals 0.
Largest of two: compare with greater than.
Largest of three: compare step by step, or use a built in max.
Grade from marks: an elif chain from highest to lowest.
Leap year: divisible by 4, and not by 100 unless also by 400.

blocks.text: A very common decision is asking whether a value falls within a range, like a score between 0 and 100.

codes.python:
score = 85
if 0 <= score <= 100:       # Python allows this clean chained form
    print("Valid score")

# in other languages, use two conditions joined with and
if score >= 0 and score <= 100:
    print("Valid score")

blocks.text: Python lets you chain the comparison in one readable line. Other languages join the two comparisons with and. Both mean the same thing.
Checking Against Many Options
When you want to know if a value is one of several options, the in operator is far cleaner than a long chain of or.
Compare that to writing day equals Saturday or day equals Sunday. The in version is shorter and easier to extend with more options.
A flag is a boolean variable that remembers a decision so you can act on it later. It is one of the most useful patterns in all of programming.
You set the flag to false to start, flip it to true when something happens, and check it afterwards. Simple and powerful.
A Real World Example: Access Control
Deciding what a user is allowed to do is pure conditionals. Here is a simple access rule.

codes.python:
logged_in = True
is_admin = False
is_owner = True

if logged_in and (is_admin or is_owner):
    print("You may edit this page")
else:
    print("You do not have permission")

blocks.text: Notice the brackets. The user must be logged in, and also be either an admin or an owner. Brackets make that rule crystal clear.

content.title: 9. A Worked Example: A Tiny Calculator

blocks.text: Let us combine input, operators, and conditionals into one small program that acts like a calculator.
The program reads two numbers and an operation, then uses an elif chain to decide which calculation to run. This tiny example already feels like a real tool.
Avoiding Repeated Checks
If you find yourself writing the same condition several times, compute it once, store it in a well named variable, and reuse it.

codes.python:
age = 20
country = "India"
is_eligible = age >= 18 and country == "India"

if is_eligible:
    print("You can register")
if is_eligible:
    print("You can vote")

blocks.text: Naming a condition makes your code read like plain English and means you only have to get the rule right in one place.
A robust program checks its input before trusting it. Conditionals are how you guard against values that would break the logic.
Checking for invalid or edge values first, before the main work, prevents a whole class of crashes and wrong answers.
FizzBuzz is the most famous beginner decision problem. For a number, print Fizz if it is divisible by 3, Buzz if by 5, FizzBuzz if by both, otherwise the number.
Notice the divisible by both check comes first. If it came last, a number like 15 would match Fizz first and never reach FizzBuzz. Order is everything.

items: Using one equals sign instead of two inside a condition
Getting the order of an elif chain wrong so an early case swallows others
Forgetting the else, so nothing happens when the condition is false
Wrong indentation in Python, which changes what belongs inside the if
Deeply nested ifs that become impossible to follow

blocks.text: When a decision goes wrong, print the condition and the values it uses. Seeing the true or false result next to the values usually reveals the mistake.
What is the difference between if and elif?
elif is checked only when the earlier if and elifs were false. It lets you handle several exclusive cases where exactly one should run.
Do I always need an else?
No. Use else only when you want something to happen when the condition is false. Many ifs stand alone.
Can I check two things at once?
Yes. Combine conditions with and or or. Use and when both must hold, or when either is enough.
Why does the wrong branch run?
Often the elif order is wrong, or a condition uses the wrong operator. Print the values and walk through the conditions top to bottom.

items: Condition: an expression that is true or false.
Branch: one of the paths a conditional can take.
elif: an extra condition checked when earlier ones were false.
Ternary: a one line choice between two values.
Truthy or falsy: non boolean values treated as true or false.
Read a number and print whether it is positive, negative, or zero.
Read three numbers and print the largest.
Read marks and print a grade using an elif chain.
Check whether a year is a leap year.
Read a day name and print whether it is a weekday or weekend.

blocks.text: Decisions let a program choose. Next you will learn to repeat work automatically with loops, and that is where programs truly come alive.
